(Photo by Wojtek RADWANSKI / AFP) Content Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Flip Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski has warned that mounting economic and military pressure on Russia could make Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin increasingly dangerous, saying Moscow should end its “criminal misadventure” in Ukraine “before it’s too late.” “The Russian economy is beginning to suffer. Russians can’t pretend that it’s an external, special military operation anymore,” Sikorski said in an interview with TVP World’s On the Record program on Tuesday. JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . But Sikorski cautioned against interpreting Russia’s growing difficulties as meaning the threat from Moscow is disappearing. “A sick man with a gun is still a man with a gun,” he said. “That’s why we are spending so much money on defense, in order to convince Putin that any conflict with Poland would cost him even more dearly than his criminal war with Ukraine.” Advertisement The Polish foreign minister said Putin’s “desperate” situation could push him to do “something risky,” as speculation grows over whether Moscow could seek to escalate the war before possible negotiations. Could Russia expand the war beyond Ukraine? Asked about warnings that Russia could eventually expand the conflict further west, Sikorski acknowledged the debate over whether some of those fears have become exaggerated. But he made clear that Warsaw cannot afford to assume Putin will behave rationally. Other Topics of Interest US Senate Delivers Overwhelming 86-12 Bipartisan Backing for Russia Sanctions as Zelensky Watches Zelensky’s Capitol visit coincides with a decisive push to squeeze Moscow’s energy revenues and raise the cost to Russia of continuing the war. “If Putin does something irresponsible, like the invasion of Ukraine, we will respond – definitely, ourselves,” Sikorski said. “His capabilities are clearly less than we had thought, but his intent is even worse.” That assessment, he suggested, is based partly on what the war has revealed about the limits of Russian military power compared with expectations before the full-scale invasion. At the same time, Sikorski argued that Putin’s intentions have proven more aggressive than many Western governments anticipated. Advertisement “He clearly doesn’t have a realistic picture of the geopolitical situation and his prospects,” Sikorski said. He described Putin as “clearly misinformed,” arguing that a Russian leader with an accurate understanding of Moscow’s situation would have greater reason to seek a deal. “The question is whether Putin is ready for a deal,” Sikorski said. Escalate before de-escalating? Sikorski was also asked about the possibility that Russia could intensify the war precisely as preparations for eventual negotiations accelerate – effectively attempting to escalate before de-escalating. The discussion also turned to the risk of further Russian escalation, including broader use of North Korean troops and a possible new mobilization drive after Russia’s September elections. Sikorski said North Korean forces are already part of Moscow’s war effort under the military treaty between Russia and North Korea. He noted that the Kremlin claims the Ukrainian territories it occupies are Russian territory – a position Moscow could use to justify deploying North Korean troops there under the agreement. “That’s a very nasty example of collaboration between two authoritarian countries,” Sikorski said, questioning what Pyongyang is receiving in return for the losses suffered among North Korean personnel. Advertisement He also challenged the assumption that another Russian draft would automatically strengthen Moscow’s forces. Conscripts, he argued, are fundamentally different from contract soldiers who voluntarily sign up to fight, making a new mobilization potentially more politically and militarily risky for the Kremlin. For Warsaw, the larger concern is therefore not simply whether Moscow has enough military capacity for another major escalation, but whether a Russian leadership under increasing pressure could nevertheless decide to take a dangerous gamble. Sikorski said the possibility that Putin “may be desperate and may do something risky” should not be dismissed. Russia weaker than feared, but still dangerous The comments underline an apparent paradox in Poland’s assessment of Russia after more than four years of full-scale war. Moscow has failed to demonstrate the level of conventional military power many Western governments feared before February 2022. But for countries on NATO’s eastern flank, that does not automatically translate into greater security. Instead, an economically strained Russia facing continued Ukrainian resistance and growing pressure on its energy sector could become less predictable. Advertisement Sikorski’s warning comes as Poland continues to invest heavily in its armed forces and deterrence against Russia, with Warsaw portraying those expenditures as necessary to ensure that Moscow understands the cost of any confrontation with a NATO member. Sikorski welcomes shift in Washington Sikorski also pointed to what he sees as an encouraging shift in Washington’s approach to the war. “The fact the US has now recognized that Ukraine has cards and made extraordinarily successful efforts to level the playing field is a good sign,” he said. His comments came as Zelensky visited Washington on Tuesday for the funeral of late Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham, one of Ukraine’s most vocal supporters in Congress. Zelensky also held a private meeting with US President Donald Trump at the White House, where the two discussed efforts to revive negotiations with Russia and Ukraine’s push for an agreement allowing it to produce Patriot missile interceptors domestically. ‘Honor’ Graham with Russia sanctions Sikorski specifically called on Trump to follow the change in rhetoric with stronger economic measures against Moscow. He said he hoped Trump would “honor” Graham by finally adopting additional sanctions against Russia. The US Senate on Tuesday was preparing to begin consideration of a bipartisan Russia sanctions package that Graham had spent his final days trying to advance. The legislation is aimed particularly at reducing the energy revenues that continue to finance Moscow’s war. http://www.bignewsnetwork.com/news/27925.text: Big News Network.com Ukraine at 35: How a countrys population halved in three decades A nation with 52 million inhabitants at independence in 1991 now has a population comparable to wartime levels under Nazi occupation After years of conflict and political and economic instability, Ukraine is now standing on the precipice of a demographic disaster. Its population has fallen by more than 40% since 1991 - the year it declared independence from the Soviet Union. A country of nearly 52 million inhabitants in 1991 - a figure comparable to the UK population at the time - is now home to fewer than 30 million, with some estimates putting the number as low as 22 million. The figure is comparable to the estimates for World War II, when Soviet Ukraine reeled under Nazi occupation, amid widespread famine, indiscriminate killings and the systematic deportation of hundreds of thousands of people to Germany for slave labor. In 2026, the country is being hollowed out from several directions at once. While many have perished on the battlefield, millions more have fled abroad - many of them young workers, women and children - while birth rates collapsed far below replacement level. Yet Ukraine's demographic hole began long before 2022. It was dug over decades by the post-Soviet economic collapse, low fertility, high mortality, emigration, and political instability. Did Ukraine have a bad start? Ukraine is no stranger to demographic catastrophes. Millions died during the Soviet famine of 1932-33, and the country suffered enormous losses during World War II. Ukraine's population stood at an estimated 41 million in 1941, but fell to around 22-23 million in 1942 during the Nazi and Romanian occupation. However, its population subsequently recovered: official Ukrainian statistics put it at 37 million in 1951 and almost 52 million in 1991. The collapse of the Soviet Union - as in many other former republics - broke the upward trend. Economic downfall, low birth rates, high mortality, and emigration pushed the population into sustained decline from the early 1990s. Independent Ukraine's first - and so far only - census, conducted in December 2001, found that the country had 48.46 million residents. The demographic problem became far worse after the Western-backed coup in Kiev in 2014, when Crimea joined Russia following a public referendum and the Donbass republics declared independence. In late 2019, a government population survey concluded that more than 37 million people were living in the territory Ukraine de facto controlled. COVID-19 delivered another blow to Ukraine, with the death toll exceeding 100,000. However, all these problems were dwarfed by the consequences of Kiev's conflict with Moscow. Where did millions of Ukrainians go? The start of full-scale hostilities triggered a massive exodus. In May 2026, Foreign Minister Andrey Sibiga estimated that as many as eight million Ukrainians had left the country. Over 5.5 million Ukrainians fled to Russia during 2022 and 2023, including more than 749,000 children, according to TASS. Ukrainians continued to arrive in Russia after 2023, although subsequent flows were counted in the tens of thousands rather than millions. To the west, refugees swamped neighboring EU countries, putting strain on local welfare systems. A total of 4.41 million people who fled Ukraine held temporary protection status in the EU as of 2026, with Germany, Poland and the Czech Republic hosting the most people. Women and children accounted for nearly three-quarters of the total. Many men have also attempted to flee the country amid Ukraine's forced mobilization campaign, which has repeatedly produced highly publicized street altercations. Others trying to leave illegally have resorted to taking dangerous routes through remote terrain, with dozens dying in the attempt. How many Ukrainians are actually left in Ukraine? Nobody knows exactly, as the last census took place 25 years ago, forcing the authorities to rely on indirect data ever since. According to Ella Libanova, director of the Ptukha Institute of Demography at the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine, about 29 million people were living in government-controlled territory in 2026, although she said the estimate could vary by about 300,000. The figure is disputed, however, with Social Policy Minister Denis Ulyutin putting the population at just 22-25 million and describing the demographic situation as a "catastrophe." What have battlefield losses done to Ukraine? Apart from refugees, Ukraine is also losing enormous amounts on people - mostly men of working age - on the battlefield. According to the Russian military, Ukraine has suffered more than 1.5 million casualties ; the figure includes those killed and wounded. Vladimir Zelensky, however, presented a wildly different account, recently claiming that Ukraine has suffered "about 50,000 soldiers killed and... about 400,000 wounded," while admitting that "a huge number" of troops simply "disappeared." In addition, more than 16,000 Ukrainian civilians have been killed in the conflict since 2022, according to UN data. Moscow maintains it never targets civilians. Do Ukrainian refugees plan on returning? Even if the guns fell silent tomorrow, it is highly unlikely that everyone who fled Ukraine after 2022 will return. Vasily Voskoboinik, head of Ukraine's Office of Migration Policy, estimates that only 10-15% of Ukrainians currently abroad may return home after the fighting ends. "The end of the war does not mean that Ukrainians will immediately start packing their things and returning to Ukraine," Voskoboinik said in March, adding that the process could take several months or even a year. He noted that while security is the main precondition for return migration, Ukraine will also have to compete with what the EU offers refugees in terms of housing, jobs and the broader quality of life - standards to which many Ukrainians have already grown accustomed. He also believes that the EU will seek to retain Ukrainians who are working and have integrated into local society, while seeking to get rid of those who remain dependent on refugee benefits. The expert estimates that out of around 6.5 million Ukrainians living in Europe, between 200,000 and one million people could return during the first two years after the end of the conflict. A 2026 Centre for Economic Strategy poll gave a more optimistic assessment, suggesting that 43% of Ukrainian refugees definitely or probably intend to return, while 36% said they probably or definitely would not. OK, the numbers are bleak. But does the problem end there? Far from it. Ukraine is not merely hemorrhaging people - the population left behind is becoming older and increasingly difficult for a shrinking workforce to support. Before 2022, State Statistics Service data put the economically active population at roughly 16-17 million, compared with around 11-11.5 million pensioners - about 1.5 economically active people for every senior citizen. According to Voskoboinik, the balance has deteriorated since then. By his estimate, Ukraine now has only about 5.5 million taxpayers, while the number of pensioners remains close to 10 million. "It turns out that now we have two pensioners for every one working person," he said. Emigration has made that imbalance harder to correct. Many of those who left are children, younger women and working-age adults, while older Ukrainians are generally less mobile. That means the exodus has removed not only current workers but also future taxpayers and potential parents, accelerating a demographic ageing process that was already well underway before 2022. What are demographic projections for Ukraine? Under the UN's World Population Prospects 2024 scenario, Ukraine's population is projected to fall to about 32.2 million by 2050 and just 15.3 million by 2100 . If that projection materializes, a country that entered independence with almost 52 million people would end the century with less than a third of that population - and fewer inhabitants than present-day Romania. Bottom Line Ukraine has spent more than three decades losing people, with the conflict accelerating every negative trend at once - deaths, emigration, collapsing births, ageing and a shrinking workforce. Even if the fighting stopped overnight, peace alone would not bring millions of refugees home. Ukraine - one of the poorest and most corrupt countries in Europe - would still have to compete for its own citizens with a much wealthier EU, where many have already built new lives. Photograph: Mohammed Huwais/AFP/Getty Images Yemen UAE agrees with Saudi Arabia to re-enter Yemen conflict amid Houthi gains United Arab Emirates will reportedly resume payments to Yemeni forces as gains by Iran-backed Houthi fighters alarm Gulf state rulers Yemen civil war: what sparked latest escalation and who is involved? Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor Sat 17 Oct 2026 07.57 EDT Last modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 10.46 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The United Arab Emirates has agreed to re-enter the Yemen conflict by resuming payments to some government forces fighting Iran-aligned Houthis in the south, according to sources in Yemen. In return, Saudi Arabia has agreed to provide air cover for the anti-Houthi force. The new cooperation agreement is the first tangible sign that the deep rift between the UAE and Saudi Arabia over Yemen’s future is starting to be healed – if only because the advance by Houthi forces across Yemen has alarmed all the rival Gulf state rulers. Saudi Arabia is facing daily drone and missile attacks and is struggling to maintain an atmosphere of normality, as Houthi strikes immobilise its airports and some of its energy infrastructure. Southern forces – mainly in the Giant Brigades – were previously trained and funded by the UAE, and are regarded as some of the most effective in the disjointed anti-Houthi military coalition. But the UAE quit operations inside Yemen in January, cutting off its funding supply line. Neither Saudi Arabia nor the UAE have responded to a demand this week by southern Yemen separatists for a referendum on secession, a move that would restore the 1967-1990 borders, when Yemen was two separate states. View image in fullscreen Yemeni Southern Giants Brigades fighters celebrate and wave their weapons. Photograph: Yemen Giants Brigades Media Centre/AFP/Getty Images The separatist Southern Transition Council has also not yet agreed for its troops to fight outside the borders of the old Southern Yemen, but an explicit agreement by Saudi Arabia to allow a referendum would be likely to lead to the lifting of that restriction. Yemen’s UN-recognised government, based in Aden, declared last week a counteroffensive to drive Houthi forces from the capital Sana’a, but so far the military drive has met with limited success around Majzar near Marib and the Bab al-Mandab strait. There is also no direct contact between the STC leader, Aidarous al-Zubaidi, and Saudi officials. Zubaidi fled to Abu Dhabi in January after a failed STC attempt to take charge across the south and announce a referendum on separation in two years’ time. In response, the Saudis bombed UAE arms shipments for STC forces. The UAE then announced it was quitting all involvement in Yemen , and the Saudi-backed government said it would seek to try Zubaidi for treason. Food and fuel run low as besieged Yemeni city braces for Houthi breakthrough Read more UAE officials are deeply concerned by the state of the conflict. Despite massive losses, the Houthis are determined eventually to capture Taiz and Marib, the two remaining cities outside the boundaries of the old Southern Yemen. On Friday two missiles fired by the Houthis struck the airport of Aden while a passenger plane was preparing to take off. No casualties were reported. The missiles landed about 500 metres from the Yemenia Airways aircraft, and approximately 100 metres from the midpoint of the runway, said Yemen’s information minister, Moammar Al-Eryani. The strike came a day after at least five people were killed and 16 injured in a Houthi attack on a presidential palace in Aden. Egypt’s president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, said he was convening an emergency session of parliament to grant his country’s military the powers to take action in defence of Saudi Arabia. He stressed Egypt would not be taking any offensive action, and would only defend Saudi Arabia. In the UK, discussions are continuing about a Saudi request for further military aid. The UK has sent an RAF Voyager air-to-air refuelling aircraft, but regional diplomats are pressing for the UK to do more. Some concern is being expressed over whether Riyadh should be engaging more closely with other Gulf States, including Oman and Qatar, on the issue. The legal implications of a blanket UK backing for the largely Saudi air campaign is also being considered, since the court of appeal in 2019 found the UK had acted unlawfully in issuing arms export licences during a previous Saudi bombing campaign of Yemen in 2015-16. The Campaign Against Arms Trade said the UK had made no proper assessment of potential Saudi breaches of international humanitarian law, forcing the UK to revise its procedures. Saudi Arabia claims to have revised its methods substantially since then, and certainly argues that it is acting in self-defence in line with the UN charter. The UN security council on 15 October adopted a UN presidential statement on 15 October asserting Saudi Arabia’s right to act in self-defence in line with international law. No accurate death toll in the war since August is available, but more than 200,000 people have been displaced, according to the UN, which is placing increasing pressure on Aden-based humanitarian groups. Open the full Ask Rio Times → Who Holds Power Today Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs, a businessman and leader of the United List alliance, leads Latvia’s government. He took office on 28 May 2026 after Evika Siliņa, the New Unity prime minister, resigned on 14 May. This guide is part of The Rio Times series on European politics . See also our guides to Spain and Germany’s AfD debate . President Edgars Rinkēvičs, in office since 8 July 2023, is head of state. His role is largely ceremonial, but the constitution gives him one decisive power: he chooses who tries to form a government. On 6 October 2026, after consulting all six parties that won seats, Rinkēvičs asked Kulbergs to do exactly that. Kulbergs therefore holds both the job and the mandate, but he still needs a parliamentary majority to keep it. How the System Works Latvia is a parliamentary republic. The Saeima has 100 members elected by proportional representation, and a party needs 5% of the vote to enter. The president is chosen by parliament, not by voters. The prime minister and cabinet need the Saeima’s confidence, so any government must command at least 51 seats. Voters last went to the polls on Saturday 3 October 2026 to elect the 15th Saeima. Turnout was 51.79%, the lowest in Latvia’s modern history and down from 59.41% in 2022. The new parliament holds its first sitting on Tuesday 3 November, when the sitting government formally hands back its mandate. The next regular election is due in autumn 2030, four years after this one. The Election Result, Seat by Seat United List won 41 seats with about 35% of the vote, almost three times its 2022 total of 15. It is an alliance that includes the Latvian Green Party, the Latvian Association of Regions and the Liepāja Party. Latvia First, a populist list, took 17 seats. Sovereign Power and the Alliance of Young Latvians, another populist list, won 15. National Alliance, a nationalist conservative party, and the Progressives, a liberal party, each won 10. New Unity, the centre-right party of former prime minister Siliņa, fell to 7. Six forces entered parliament in total. No other party cleared the 5% bar. The Fight to Build a Majority Kulbergs announced that formal talks would open on Wednesday 28 October with the National Alliance and New Unity, his partners in the outgoing four-party coalition. Both were part of the cabinet he has led since May. United List with those two would hold 58 seats, a comfortable majority. United List with National Alliance alone would hold exactly 51, the bare minimum. The arithmetic matters, because United List and New Unity together would hold only 48 seats, short of a majority. National Alliance is therefore the partner Kulbergs cannot do without. A new cabinet needs the Saeima’s confidence vote, so the talks must produce at least 51 seats. The cabinet that Kulbergs led since May included the Union of Greens and Farmers, a rural-based party, which is not named as a first-choice partner this time. Where Latvia Stands on the EU, NATO and Russia Latvia is a member of both the European Union and NATO, and it shares borders with Russia and Belarus. Latvia has backed Ukraine with military and financial aid since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. A law passed by the Saeima in March 2026 requires defence spending of at least 5% of GDP from 2027. That target matches the level that Washington has urged on NATO allies. Kulbergs has also promised tougher scrutiny of two costly state projects: airBaltic, the national airline, and Rail Baltica, a railway link to Poland. The railway is meant to connect the Baltic states with western Europe. Economy and the 2027 Budget The European Commission’s spring 2026 forecast put Latvia’s budget deficit at 3.3% of GDP in 2026 and 4.3% in 2027. The jump reflects the rise in defence spending. The 2027 budget is the first test for any new cabinet. Whoever governs will have to balance defence, cost-cutting and promises to voters. What It Means for US Readers For investors, Latvia is a small euro-area economy whose bonds and companies trade in euros, so the main risk is policy, not currency. A stable majority that keeps budget discipline would reassure lenders, while a fragile one could delay the 2027 budget. For security, Latvia is a frontline NATO state that has legally committed to the 5% of GDP defence goal Washington asks of allies from 2027. American travellers face no new restrictions from the election, and the border with Belarus remains a security-sensitive area. What Is Not Known It is not known which parties will finally join the coalition, or whether talks with National Alliance and New Unity will succeed. Nor is it known whether Kulbergs will bring in a fourth party, or how ministries will be shared. It is also unclear how long the talks will take, and what the 2027 budget will contain.
